The cashier glanced at the accountant. The accountant glanced at Pranav-sir, who was on the phone and kept talking. A farmer at the counter looked at all of them and stayed in his chair. She put the passbook down, said "Chalo, let's go out," to no one in particular, and walked to the door. Chairs scraped behind her. Within a minute, the whole branch was standing in the dusty yard beside the tea stall.

Bao noticed where everyone's eyes went: not to the exit sign, but to each other's faces, checking. The team lead was still on a video call, nodding. Nobody wanted to be the one who overreacted. Bao felt the same pull and stayed seated, heart ticking faster. Then Kwame, who sat by the window, stood, pulled on his jacket and said, "I'm not dying for a spreadsheet." He headed for the stairs. It was like a spell breaking. In thirty seconds half the floor was in the stairwell, laughing nervously, and Bao was among them.

The team lead kept talking to a customer, so the rest of us kept talking to customers. I actually said, "Sorry, sir, there's some noise here." Today at 11 am the fire alarm rang. I watched from the supervisor desk. Not one agent stood. Headsets stayed on. Saurabh, on a call, looked up, saw nobody moving, and kept talking. I could see people glancing at each other, each waiting for someone else. I waited too, for about twenty seconds, which I am not proud of. Next steps: I will run an unannounced drill next month, and each row will have a named person whose job is to stand first.

Tarun
